div.p: Tape #6R Interviewer: Maura Marchand (M) Interviewees: Harry Bingaman (H) and Dorothy Bingaman s(D) Date: April 15, 1974. Place: residence, Laurelton, Pa.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So this will give you a little idea of some of the subjects we're interested in, but maybe to start off, I hear you've learned to quilt.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: That's right, I, well, I had seen my mother do quilting and seen other people do it, but when I had a mental breakdown, my doctor advised me to do something to keep busy, so she had some guilt tops here that her mother had made, and we had some that my mother had made, and we decided to begin putting them together and quilting them, and that's how I got into it, so I'm really involved now. I do as many as, oh, I'd say, from twelve to fifteen quilts every winter, don't I?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Um huh.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, my goodness, and you really turn. . . . H:.. and that's just the quilting. I . . I. . . she does the putting the tops together.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Piecing?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, the piecing. Now, I...well, actually, perhaps you'd like to know something about the history of quilting...

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I would.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
I think, from what I gather, from what I've read, quilting is an art that has evolved from a necessity. In the early colonial days, the people had to have plenty of warm clothing for their beds, and I understand that they stuffed their quilts with all varieties of things, even leaves. A quilt was filled with leaves and then knotted--they couldn't quilt it as well--but they had been knotted, and it became a com¬ forter then. . . or paper, or. . . well, cotton came into the picture somewhat later, when they began growing cotton in America, but wool was one of the things that they used quite prevalently, and even old rags that couldn't be used in the making of a quilt. Quilt making, somebody has given it a definition that quilt making is the making of cloth from small scraps of cloth. Actually, that's the piece-work quilt, and the earliest type of a guilt was the crazy quilt, which was all kinds of patches and all shapes of patches fitted together haphazardly and finally to make up the quilt. Somehow later, I'm not just sure when, they began to develop the idea of making blocks, making a design into a block, and then fitting the blocks together, to make up another design, an intricate design from the blocks that were used. But it is quite interesting to note that this thing started as a necessity, because people needed heavy covers. Now we talked today about--and I have made, I haven't made any king-size. . . I have made queen-size--we did do a king-size for the Becks at Northumberland, wasn't that a
king-size...?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Um huh.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: I think it was. We talk about this as new, making king¬ size quilts . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Yes, I'd say so.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
. . . but from the reading that I've done, I've discovered that the beds were a natural-size bed, but they were so high, and then underneath the bed they kept a trundle bed for the other. children in the family to sleep in, so in order to hide the trundle bed, the quilt was made large enough that it reached the floor on both sides of the bed, so that actually you had a king-size quilt in those early days, as well, for that purpose. Now, there's three kinds of quilts. Actually, the piece-work quilt, which is taking small pieces of cloth, fitting them into a design and putting it together--we call that patchwork sometimes, but that isn't actually the patchwork. The patchwork is the applique type of guilt, because —it got the name of patchwork because when you patched a garment, you laid a patch on top of the garment and stitched it fast. And that's how the applique quilt came to be known as a patchwork quilt. Then the third type of quilt is the all white plain guilt, which doesn't show any patchwork or piecework on it, it's just all worked out with a design of quilting, and that usually is made with a central design of some important effect, and then branching out from that to
fill the entire white area. I made one like that for the George Becks of Northumberland, and I started with their monogram, the "B', in the middle, and then branched out with all types of designs to fit into the quilt. Now, in early days, well, when my mother was young, when they quilted, they did very intricate quitting, the quilting was done at least about an inch apart, the rows of quilting, for the simple reason that when they used cotton wadding or cotton filling, it had to be quilted that close together or when it was washed it would just wad together.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, year, the reason for all these things . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
So now, with the invention of dacron batting, it does not have to be quilted that closely, and it doesn't have to be the criss-cross quilting all the time—you can work in beautiful designs in your quilting now. I also wanted to mention the fact that people who didn't have an all-white quilt sometimes would turn their guilt over on the opposite side and use the back of it as an all-white quilt. Quilts were used for, oh, various purposes, mostly for keeping warm, but there was a type of guilt which has been very interesting to me, and we have one of them. It is called the mourning quilt. When a person died out in the country, they didn't take the body to the undertaking establishment. They usually did the whole process of embalming or whatever was necessary, or whatever they knew at that time, in the home. And then when they laid
out the corpse--I don't like that word, anyway, but that's..

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Right, well, dead body... H:..when they laid out the dead person on the bed, they covered them what they called the mourning quilt, which was usually a black--predominantly black--quilt, and we have that her grandmother made, which was the mourning quilt-- it was used for that purpose. Now, in early days when they used the used the crazy guilt design, they usually went around the borders of each patch, with a type of embroidery stitching, the feather stitch was quite often used all around in those kinds of quilts. Then later people began to collect velvet patches and made velvet patches into quilts, and those quilt¬ are always done with embroidery around the edges. Then, of course, most of those quilts, instead of being quilted then, they are--the thread is pulled through and knotted and tied, which they call a knotted quilt, which in actual parlance is a comforter and not a quilt, because the quilting is...

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab:
. . . is not there. H: . . . gives it the name of the quilt. Quilting actually started in China and Mongolia many, many years--well, I guess, before Marco Polo ever made his trips, because it is said that Marco Polo brought back quilted garments from the Orient, when he made some of his trips there. An interesting thing about quilts, also--the quilting--in the early days was used for warmth, because most of those countries were cold countries, but they were used for protection, as well. It is said that a
quilted garment worn by a warrior would blunt an arrow, that an arrow oftentimes wouldn't go through the garment they were wearing, so it was a good thing for protection, as well. Now I don't know what else I could. . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Maybe we could return for a minute to the featherstitch. Now if you could tell me a little bit about the featherstitch . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, I don't know if you know what the featherstitch is. It's a stitch that--the stitch goes out one direction on the one side and then it's turned the other to make a . . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: What, it's sort of a series of . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah, a zigzag.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Okay, I believe I've seen it . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah, you probably have.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now I was wondering about--you talk about the early history and you mentioned that they started backing them with cotton. Do you have any idea like about when they were starting to back them with cotton, or like when the crazy quilt pattern was started. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Well, I--well, cotton was begun to be grown in the South in the early seventeen-hundreds or middle seventeen-hundreds, I would think, and incidentally, I don't know if this is any connection with it or not, but Britain--England--put on taxes--the taxes on cloth were higher than the taxes on tea. We often say in history--American history-- that we fought the American Revolution over a tax on tea. The taxes on cloth were higher, because England was making cloth. Now, England wasn't making
cotton cloth then--the woolen cloth, and the linen with the flax--so that when the American colonies began growing cotton, England at one time had a law against importing cotton into England. Now, what they were doing in America for a while was making cloth out of cotton and sending it to England, and then they passed laws against that, too, in England, because they wanted to sell to the Colonies, not buy from them, to a great extent. So that--that's one of the things that--so cotton began to be used quite profusely by the end of the seventee-hundreds. By the time our War of Independence was on, I think, we were pretty well established with cotton.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, how about when you mention your parents doing quilting-- did they learn the quilting from their parents . . . ?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Very likely--I kind of think so, yes, and in the early days, too, they had what they called the quilting parties or quilting bees. It was one of the things—one of the social events- of the season, I guess, where people would get together. The men would come along to the quitting bee and the men would get together and talk their talk, and the women had a chance to talk their talk and still do the job of quilting.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, did both the men and the women participate in the quilting then, or was it mainly . . . ?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Well, I presume, they must have, because somewhere I was reading that quite a long time ago men began to be interested in doing the quilting as well as the women, but, of course, men were used to doing outdoor work and their hands were rough and you
don't want rough hands when you're working with thread or that sort of thing. But I also read a story one time where some young man was courting a certain girl and they held hands underneath the guilt while they were quitting, so apparently the men did aid in quitting. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Verification that at least he was sitting there, if he wasn't quilting.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Presumably, she wasn't doing much either.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Yes, it would be rather hard to guilt with just one hand. Oh,well...

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: I read in one book about the process of quilting, and they said that the quilting was done by holding the left hand under the guilt and pushing the needle through, and when it hurt, you knew the needle was through. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: And then the left hand would . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, the left hand—one way that they used to do quilting was push the needle down through and pull it through and then push it up again, but I do my running stitch by running it through and up, and many quilters do the same way. I've watched quilters down at Kutztown Fair, and they do that.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, I don't--you still. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Push the needle down through with one hand and bring it up at the same time, but you guide it up with this other hand underneath, so that you do one stitch and pull your needle on up, instead of pulling it all the way down.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Um huh, that would be faster.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now your stretch going down would be vertical, but your stitch coming up may not be totally vertical, because you're. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: No--yeah . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: . . . because you're pulling at an angle. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: You don't want you're--the quilt shouldn't be stretched too lightly on the frame--they don't stretch them out too tightly for that purpose, so that you have some give. Then if you push the needle down and then zigzag it up, it has room to give.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Is it-did it take you a long time to make your stretching totally consistent?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Well, when we first started I told my wife--she said I was making pretty large stitches, and I said, well, if anybody makes them any smaller, than that, you gotta show me. So she went and got one of the quilts that her grandmother had made, and showed that they did do finer stitches than--I have improved; it gradually came that--actually, one book that I read stated that seven or eight stitches to the inch was good, but I have on numerous occasions made more than that to the inch, so they are finer--depending upon the thickness of your material that you're working with. For instance, if you're working with a-- when we make the all plain white quilt--all that you have is-- there's no seems there, you see, to go through with your needle, and you can do finer stitches on that type of work. And then the
dacron batting that we use today sprays a whole lot farther than cotton does, and you can make smaller stitches with the dacron batting, too.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, do you always stitch in the same color thread? I mean like as the fabric?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: No, it's usually done with white thread. I like to work with white thread, but some quilts are used-- are made with colored thread. You can buy the quilting thread in colors as well as white.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, now, quilting thread is separate from...

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Quilting thread is made a little stronger, with the same heaviness of a regular about a #50 thread.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, where can I buy that?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, at various stores.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Old Trail?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Bowen's? Did somebody say Bowman's had it? I get mine right now down at Ben Franklin's. They have it. Penney's have always had it.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Because I've just gotten with the thread they're selling. You know, it breaks without even looking at it.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Well, the thing that cracks me up right now in the thread business is thread has suddenly jumped to sixty cents a spool. I'm still able to get it down at Ben Franklin for forty-five, but when we started out what was it? Twenty-nine, wasn't it? Twenty-nine cents for a spool of thread when we first started doing quilting--that's only a few years ago. Now it's up to sixty.
So, you talk about inflation, then--we've bought in the quilting

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Right there you go out and buy as much as you can for for forty-five cents (unintelligible) How about patterns and things?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, patterns for quilting are made in floral designs and zigzag designs, all kinds of designs, and I usually--now, in the old days they used to take a pin and mark their pattern on the cloth, by scratching with that pin would make a line. Well, I usually just use pencil--that's what they use--I've watched the ladies at Kutztown Fair quilting, and they do theirs with pencil.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, does that pencil wash out?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Gradually, it washes out, yes. I use dressmaker's pencils, too--marked pencils. If I have a dark patch that pencil wouldn't show up on, I use a light...

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Chalk.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . chalk pencil.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So a lot of the designs you've designed--a lot of that patterns you've designed yourself?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: A lot of the patterns I've designed myself, and a lot of them are patterns that we have picked from people who have done quilting. An old friend of ours over by Danville gave us a quilting frame--our first quitting frame--no, not our first one...

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: No, not our first one.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Aunt Nora gave us a quilting frame and gave us some of her patterns, and another lady that we knew had done quilting,
When she passed at her sale we bought some other materials, and among the materials were her quitting patterns. Cardboard is what they use to make the patterns out of of --cut them so that they are substantial. You can buy them now made of metal.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Well, we have some of rubber.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: The old times, those are the old timers.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I heard that some old ones were made of tin.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, yes, we have some tin, we bave some metal...

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yes, we have some tins.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: (unintelligible)

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: The Quilter's Newsletter is selling--they advertise quilt patterns for making--and the tin plates for making the blocks for patching--for piecing the quilt. They make those, too. Now, the patterns for the pieced quilts--oringinally I said the first one, I think, very likely was the . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Crazy quilt?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . . crazy quilt design, and then they began taking square blocks and putting them together. One of the oldest block designs is the nine-patch, which is a block with nine squares, and you'd work that out in various colors--well, in fact, I have one in the frame in there now that's a nine-patch that you can look at.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I'd like to see it. This is where they take nine small squares and put them together and make a larger square?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Yes. Not only--well, sometimes they use small squares and then
they'd add a square about that large. This one in here, I would say it's about nine inches square, so that each individual is about three inches, I think, in this one here. So they may have been various sizes. Originally when they started making block designs, they would make a block--quite large block-- and the original quilts had four of those on them, just four, and then had a border added. Now, there's another interesting thing that has been added to the quilt--sometimes the blocks when they are put together are divided by a path of material-- sometimes white material, or other colored material to separate the block from the next block. Then they added around the whole bunch of blocks--they added what they called in quitting the rake. The rate is a different color. Then the border is added on . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So then you have your blocks, and a path, and then a rake . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . and then a rake . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: . . . and then a border, and then a binding?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . and then the binding, yes. And then oftentimes, originally, well--I don't think the folks in the old days had binding. They just folded over the edge of the material, and made a binding of that type. When it's so much easier today you buy a binding and attach it that way.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Well, that's very, very interesting. These terms--the path and the rake--were there any folk tales or stories associated with them?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
I'm not sure, but the block designs that they worked out--
--it's interesting to note that you'll pick up a quilt book and see this design and it'll give it a certain name. Then you'll pick up another book and see the same design and it has a different name. Names follow different localities. Now, there's one that--it's a crazy design; it's made up of squares and triangles and diamonds, I guess, isn't it?--made into what they call the "drunkard's path."

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I've seen them, yes.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Then there's about a dozen ways of putting the "drunkard's path' together, so that it is not always the same design.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, how do they do it in this area?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, various--I've seen a number of different methods.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Even within the like Union County area.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh, um huh. Then there's a hexagon patch--small hexagon patch--that they used, and the most that I have seen of that patch used is to make up what they call a "grandmother's flower garden," which is a patch of these hexagons starting (at?) the center and then following around them until they had a patch about that large--about a foot large or less. And then these were--there was a path put around those, usually green...

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Around the little hexagons . . . ?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Around the group of hexagons. Then they had --then, you see, there's a flower garden, and a green path around it, over here's another flower bed, and so on--that would make up "grandmother's flower garden." Now, they've taken that same nexagon patch, and started in the middle with just one patch,
and keep going 'round and lround and 'round . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, like a spiral. H; Yeah . . . and that they called a mosaic. That was called mosaic.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Um huh. Now, was this--the term "mosaic"--is that--does that go back a long time, or is that a term that's just developed recently?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: It's a long time.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: No, I think, because--I think, if you have ever noticed tile floors--I'm trying to think where I saw a tie floor that was called a mosaic, in one of the capitols somewhere where I visited, but this pattern was used, and they called it a mosaic pattern, which is a pattern which develops like that. Then there's another one that they use that hexagon--what was that one called . . . ?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Well, Marie had one that's called "Job's troubles."

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: "Job's troubles."

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: It was made--instead of round--it was made in a big diamond, and that was called "Job's troubles." And she says now, it is Job's troubles, because you can't put it together. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: It's a hard thing to put together.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: . . . without another quilt to go by.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: That's interesting Mrs. Bingaman. That's very interesting. I've seen one that's called "wedding ring," and I. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: . . . and I can't remember. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . "double wedding ring," yes . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Do they use hexagonal pieces of fabric there? D; No . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: No, they're partly--what are they?--partly circular, aren't. . . ?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Concave, sort of, to make . . . D; Yes . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . to make--I don't know.(laughter) I know it's not too difficult to make, and it's a quite popular quilt, 'cause we had a lady here a couple of weeks ago that wanted to buy a quilt, and she wondered if we had any "double wedding ring." We've never made any. I've quilted some for Mrs. Swasey at Lewisburg. I don't know if you know Mrs. Swasey or not. Her husband used to work out at the Penitenriary.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: How do you spell that?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: S-w-a-s-e-y, I think it is. She lives out on . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Buffalo Road...?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Buffalo Road, yes, near the--what used to be the Christian church. And that's quite a popular --another popular one was the "Irish chain," and that had it's variance, too. There was the "double Irish chain" and then there was the "triple Irish chain. That was made of square blocks worked into a pattern.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: And the first one started with your single . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: It was a nine-patch.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh. Yeah, that was a nine-patch square worked into a design that they called the "Irish chain."

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh. Now, are there any of these patterns that are just local in Union County, or patterns like maybe of even this little area: Laurelton? Millmont?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: I don't believe so. I think, people traded patterns, and I see by the Quilter's Newsletter magazine that they still-- people are still putting the ad in the paper wanting a certain pattern-- they'd like to trade such and such pattern for that pattern. So I think they must have done that in years back, because I know wherever we've been we see a quilt--we go to fairs and see quilts on display and stand there and draw it all so that we could make a pattern like it.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: And we saw one at the Toronto fair in Canada a number of years ago and you asked that lady and she sent you the pattern, didn't she?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: On, yes, I wrote to her, and she sent me two patterns.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: So that's how the various patterns, I think, got around, but then they would give it a name in their area, and then somebody else would--I guess they'd forget what that name was, so they'd give it a name themselves as if it originated in a certain spot, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now, there's Quilter's Newsletter magazine, is that published in Pennsylvania?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
No, that's from--where is it? It should be in the back . . .
M; I was just wondering--trying to get a feel of, you know, how large it's circulation is.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: But the lady who is editor of this magazine was at Kutztown Fair this past summer when the quilts were on display--she visited the quilting there.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: In the Kutztown Fair, are they known for their quilt?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes, yes--and they're very special prices when you see them on display--they're quite high. Of course, that's Pennsylvania Dutch, and the Pennsylvania Dutch are among the people who have kept some of these things alive You see, when the time came when by machine they could make blankets and covers a lot of people gave up doing these things, and bed the Pennsylvania Dutch, being as saving as they always have been, have kept up some of these traditions, and I think it's through the Pennsylvania Dutch we are having a revital of quilting.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Yeah, I certainly do feel that they are probably part responsible for keeping many of these crafts . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, I think so definitely, yes, and for spreading, because as they visited with each other they talk about their quilts and their new designs that they're working on.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So you've just been involved for maybe ten or fifteen years?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Just about ten years.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab:
And if you’re doing twelve or fifteen a year, you're doing
an awful lot of . . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: (laughter) Well, I have done quilts that have gone, oh, let's see--we had one that went to Scotland, but we brought it back home with us didn't we? (daughter)

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: No, it's still in Scotland.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Is it? Oh, there is one over in Scotland yet; but I have quilts that went to Arizona, Florida . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: West Virginia?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . West Virginia . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:

All handwork. I was very disappointed this week. We have a--well, she's about like an elderly lady in Mifflinburg, but she's quite ill, and she had a quilt that when she was a little girl her mother's friends gave her what we call a friendship
quilt--it's a patchwork, and then in the center's a plain white block, and they write--embroider--their names, and she wanted this put together-- bless her heart, she washed them and ironed them . . .

sp.ab: . . . and I felt bad about it, because they're just so out of shape that I was afraid to do it, because I'm not too good at it anyway, but I had to send them back, and I feel bad about it. because . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I'm sure you do.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: . . . I wanted to do it for her, but you just couldn't because, why, they would hang in a rainbow.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Um huh.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, it's very difficult with a quilt that you can't stretch out. It's very difficult to quilt without getting bags in them.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: I really don't believe that the woman understands too much about quilts, because, now, when you do a quilt nothing is washed. It all has to be new, you know.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: It should be--well, it should be.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: It should be new, or something that hasn't been laundered. And she gave us this sheet for a quilt that he'd done a couple of years ago--well, that was bad because--now, that won't shrink, but the rest will.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Right

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, if any part of it's going to be washed then it should all be washed, because--so that the shrinkage is the same.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Um huh, right.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Now, Betty Jean's worked--they were launched, but they just--she was a little careful, I guess, in how she ironed them. But, oh, it was just too bad. I hope she can get somebody else to do it, but I just was afraid to try. I really was.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: (unintelligible) . . . 'cause it's so hard. I mean, you want it to come out nice, too, and, in fact, the fabric, if it's been washed and stretched--well, you couldn't get it on to the surface, you'd have bumps and irregularities . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah, that's right--it's just too difficult.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: And it was patches that were--well, it was just . . . (unintelligible)

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: And the friendship was a very popular quilt that's the type of quilt that they usually gave to . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Brides.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
. . brides, or another interesting thing that I discovered in reading about quilting was the fact that in the early days, of course, a girl's main purpose was to get married and have a family. Well, she usually would--she was taught to sew and she would usually make the patches for a quilt but until she had a man in view or was engaged to be married or about to be married, she wasn't allowed to put that quilt together. Then they would have a party and invite her friends in and they would help her put the quilt together and that was her dowry quilt, so that she
was ready--she would at least have one quilt when she was married. Another interesting thing I noted, also in reading this one book here, that young men, when they were engaged to be married, oftentimes they would make a special quilt for him so that he had a guilt when he would get married. We've done that, we've given our children quilts.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: What book are you reading?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, this is The Perfect Patchwork Primer, by Beth Gutcheon. It's quite interesting. Most of the book is filled with designs, you see, of patchwork--how to put them together. I didn't too closely at this to see what . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: This is a new one, I just got it . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: The "Dresden plate" was one of the . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Earlier ones.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . earlier ones, too. That's a sort of a circular, longish . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Your fan quilt was an old . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: The fan was an,old one, yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: . . . was an old one.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: They originally began with square blocks and putting square blocks together. Then they began experimenting with the diamond blocks. And then when they got those worked out, then they began fitting in circular or half-circular blocks and they have,well--your "snowball" quilt is another of those that can be worked into various designs.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: That is an early quilt.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Now, another book that we have is more--is quite interesting, and that is The Romance of the Patchwork Quilt.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: It's entitled The Romance of the Patchwork Quilt?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Who wrote that, do you remember? Uh, don't worry about it.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: I don't think we have it. Here's the "grandmother's flower garden." You see the way the hexagon . . . ?

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, oh, okay . . . H: . . . started with the center and then worked out into a pattern?

sp.ab: My great grandmother made a doll blanket, and she's made a few pillows that my grandmother has now. She made a doll blanket for me when I was a very little child and I still have it. That's very pretty.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: (laughter)

sp.ab: Don't we have the book?

sp.ab: No, I think we loaned it. Didn't Molly borrow it?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Well, you have two.

sp.ab: Well, we gave one to Dora, didn't we?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Oh, then we don't have any.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Dora has the one and Molly has the other one. This lady that wrote this book talks about--somewhere in there she mentions the fact that someone a book called The Romance of the Patchwork Quilt, and she said, I assure you there was not romance to it. It was hundreds of hard-working hours put into a quilt, and that's one of the things that I'm afraid a lot of people don't realize--the work that goes into the making of
a quilt. We had a lady here some time ago that I did a quilt for her, and she said, if I were to sell this quilt I would have to have a couple of hundred dollars because she said, I have that many hours of my own work in it.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I'm sure, because I made a little Winnie the Pooh--you know, child's stories. I made a little Winnie the Pooh, and my Pooh Bear was that big—you know, fourteen, sixteen inches high--and I didn't do anything fancy and I cheated--it was an applique-type thing. I just--we have a Winnie the Pooh book and I just sort of sketched it larger on the fabric and said, well, that looks like a bear if you use a little imagination, and then I just used the sewing machine to put it on, but even cheating and using the sewing machine--and then I tied it, knotted, I guess you called it--and that took me a couple of days to just do that, and I can easily see how it just takes weeks and weeks. In fact, if you can do fifteen quilts in a winter, why, you must be sitting at that quitting bench all day long.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Why, I do . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: You always wonder--stop it and turn it back and play and see if they're recording.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Well, certainly it's been a long time for a lot of the patterns to evolve.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes.

sp.ab: Do you remember off-hand of either of your parents specifi¬ cally mentioning the certain pattern that grandmother so-and-so made or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: The fan . . .

sp.ab: The fan quilt. H; The fan quilt, the "necktie" quilt . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Neckties, that was one of the older . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.ab: Where they would actually take old neckties . . . ?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: No, it was a patch--like a bowtie . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: No, they would--it was like a bowtie.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . and they called that the "necktie."

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, okay, I think I have seen them.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah. In fact some books list it as the "bowtie" instead of the "necktie."

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yeah. Oh, my grandmother was quite a quilter.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes, in those days they had quilting bees yet.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: You see, that was her--the mourning that I had... H:... was hers.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: . . . was my great grandmother's.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . great grandmother's.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harry:

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, I believe. I believe it.

sp.speaker: Harry:

sp.speaker: Dorothy:

sp.speaker: Dorothy:

sp.speaker: Dorothy:

sp.speaker: Harry:

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Yes, when we was over . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:

sp.speaker: Dorothy:

sp.ab: The patterns seem to have such interesting names. There's "Joseph's coat," "Charlotte's crown," "double saw tooth," "clown's choice" . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Now how about the quilting itself? You mentioned that, for this gentleman in Northumberland, that you had designed a quilt—a plain white quilt—and used their monogram. Now, does the quilting itself have--I know it has various patterns -- but do the various patterns have names and . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. Yes, there are some -- "princess feather' " is one of them that is the design of a feather. In fact, I originated one that I called the "spider web" that I work into--on the plain block I use these patterns. We'll show her the baby quilt. That's still here, isn't it? Millicent's?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: The palms" is also called the "hosannah."

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: That's the story of the . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: You see, there you've got the Palm Sunday story and they had a guilt design, gave it a Bible name. Yes, there are intriguing names given to some of these patterns.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab:
There certainly are. I'm just fascinating looking at all the
patterns in this book. There's _________ than I could imagine.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: The "bear's paw" was in--it goes back to the early railroad. Do you remember the story? There's something about that. I’ll have to hunt that up.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Now, of course, when they started making applique patterns they usually cut a pattern-- when materials like chintz or some of that sort of material was made, with a printed pattern on it--they would cut that pattern out and then apply it on to a solid piece of material, and applique it on, and they would take various things like that and work that into a pattern, so that it made an interesting--the applique quilts are rather attractive, too.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Is there any problem by using a different type of fabric for applique, with the difference in shrinking or. . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Sometimes, yes. Sometimes there is that problem. Another interesting in the old days when they had--in fact, I read in that book there that the very oldest quilts had no green patches, because they had no green dye for cloth in the old colonial days. They had red and they had blue, but I still don't know why they couldn't have . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: If they had blue, I'm sure they would have had yellow and . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah, that's what I was wondering, but they said in there that that's one way they could always determine the age of the very old quilt's because there was no green in them, until they got dyes that would--they may have had green dye, but it was a dye that wouldn't stay . . .fade out.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: I was thinking of herbal dyes and things like this that they could have used . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, because . . .

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: . . . like the Indians of the Southwest.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . in the colonial days they did--well, they used onion shells to make a brown and . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Walnut . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . walnut to make a brown. Yes, walnut was used for purple, too.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Why, down at Kutztown Fair they showed how they dyed their materials with the different herbs and things like that.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Until manufactureing came along with a good process that made dyes that would stay. .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Colorfast . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . colorfast, it was tricky.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: This is really fascinating, and I just love, you know, hearing what you're telling about the histories. I really don't-- I knew very little about quilting and I . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: I can't imagine how anybody could sleep with a design like that on a quilt. (laughter).

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Makes you dizzy just looking at it.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab:
Well, so you should turn the light out and then forget about it. How about using--well, sometimes I see quilts are made like with two or with two different types of fabric. Of course, your crazy quilt's got all sorts of kinds of fabric, but often
with the piece quilts, would they use all different types of fabric or would they generally try to . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, I think they worked all fabric together, yes.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: But they don't any more.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: They don't any more, but they try to.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: They use one kind of fabric.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: But I think in those days they used whatever they had, and a garment that was worn--worn out--it was still good for quilt patches.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: I was just reading that. I was just reading that in here, in Grandma's Quilting Corner, how they—in the summertime, the things they made their clothing out of and then when it was warm a little bit they would put it in the quilts.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: What, because often like you wear the elbows out out of a shirt and the knees out of socks much faster than other. parts of the garment.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Right.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: It says, "I'll have to admit the patterns were pretty even when the quality of the material was not uniform or fine." But they used pretty feed sacks . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh. They used everything they had.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Everything--there was nothing wasted.

sp.ab: Were there any other tools used in quilt making -- you have your long frame, your cloth . . . ?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Incidentally, that's an interesting thing too about the
quilt making. We have--how many frames do we own?

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Five.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Five frames.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: What!

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: And they're all different. They're all hand-made.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: All hand-made.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Oh, my goodness!

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: These people made these things--did their own individual. .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: We have six. We have Mother Bingaman's that . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes, that's right. The one that...

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: Six.

sp.ab: ...is fitted together with clamps. That was the type they used when they had quilting bees. They'd stretch out the whole quilt on a frame and used clamps to hold the frame together to stretch it out and then everyday all around—all four sides of the quilt.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: All four sides.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: How did you do the center?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, they would roll it then. They would work in as far as they could reach and then they'd roll it in and . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: And they would have to keep that stretched pretty far, too . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Oh, yes, yes. But it mentions in there that--I think they said eight people at the most, but you could get twelve people-- you could get three people on a side--if the quilt was a good size.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab:
And this very large frame--this would go back for quite a
while?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: Um huh. Now, what about other types of frames?

sp.ab: Well, the kind I have in here now that I have a quilt in-- they were designed so that the quilt was attached to both rollers--both ends--then rolled as they were finished . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: They started in the center and . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah, they usually started in the center and worked toward the ends. In fact, that is the best way to work.

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: How would they do that?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Well, they'd roll it . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: They'd roll it. They would just have to roll it,

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: . . . roll both sides . . . .

sp.speaker: Dorothy:
sp.ab: They would unroll the one and then roll it on the other side. H:...and then roll it on the other one, um huh, yes.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: You start from the center to--so that as you work out, in case there is any--the fabric stretches or as you work . . .

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh, that's the way they used to do it. Now, when I'm working alone I start at one end, but I don't roll it on the other roller. I let it hang out over, so that it's stretched at all times for me. I mean, as I roll it in, it's stretched out, so I have no problems with bellies.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: But now if you don't put it in the other roller what keeps it taut at the other end?

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab:
Well, I use thumb tasks and keep it tacked on the other side,
and I stick my thumb tasks in where there would be quitting comes or, so that it doesn't leave a whole somewhere else.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So then you have it thumb tacked in the board at the far end of the room and you start down here and then roll it up as you move toward the other end.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Um huh.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: So that when you're first starting you're taking up the whole room.

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Maura:
sp.ab: And as you're getting closer and closer to the finish...

sp.speaker: Harry:
sp.ab: Actually, yes. I keep mine in the bedroom there where it's over at the side and it doesn't take up too much space. When we first started, we set up the frame in here. Now, when you set up a frame and it takes you two or three weeks to work a quilt, now that thing's sitting here in the middle of the living room for two or three weeks, (laughter) it's got to be a kind of a nuisance.

sp.speaker: Harry:
